Predicting plot attributes from species lists

Source: vignettes/resolveR.Rmd
resolveR.Rmd

A vegetation plot’s species list says a lot about the place it was recorded: alpine species grow high up, wetland species where the ground stays wet. RESOLVE learns this from data. It encodes the species observed in each sample into one latent representation and reads several attributes off it, here the elevation and the habitat of a plot.

This article runs the whole path on a small survey that ships with the R package: loading two tables, training a model, reading how well it predicts plots it did not train on, and predicting new plots.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/resolve/r")

# The engine library, downloaded once
library(resolveR)
resolve.install_backend()
pip install resolve-core

Installing the engine covers the GPU build, building from source and the command line.

Two tables

The survey has 150 plots in the Alps. plots holds one row per plot: its identifier, coordinates, elevation in metres and habitat. species holds one row per species recorded on a plot, with the species’ genus and family and its cover in percent. The plot identifier links the two tables.

library(resolveR)

plots <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "plots.csv", package = "resolveR"))
species <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "species.csv", package = "resolveR"))
head(plots, 3)
#>   plot_id     lat     lon elevation   habitat
#> 1    A001 46.6042 11.4453      2188    alpine
#> 2    A002 47.0674 10.5684       568 grassland
#> 3    A003 46.6674 11.3040      2129   wetland
head(species, 3)
#>   plot_id                  species        genus     family cover
#> 1    A001 Rhododendron ferrugineum Rhododendron  Ericaceae    54
#> 2    A001            Carex curvula        Carex Cyperaceae    51
#> 3    A002          Quercus petraea      Quercus   Fagaceae    16
import pandas as pd
import resolve_core as rc

data = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gcol33/resolve/master/r/inst/extdata/"
plots = pd.read_csv(data + "plots.csv")
species = pd.read_csv(data + "species.csv")
print(plots.head(3))
#>   plot_id      lat      lon  elevation    habitat
#> 0    A001  46.6042  11.4453       2188     alpine
#> 1    A002  47.0674  10.5684        568  grassland
#> 2    A003  46.6674  11.3040       2129    wetland
print(species.head(3))
#>   plot_id                   species         genus      family  cover
#> 0    A001  Rhododendron ferrugineum  Rhododendron   Ericaceae     54
#> 1    A001             Carex curvula         Carex  Cyperaceae     51
#> 2    A002           Quercus petraea       Quercus    Fagaceae     16

Loading a dataset

The roles name the columns: which one identifies the plot, which one the species, and which optional columns hold the abundance, the taxonomy and the coordinates. Each target is a column to predict, with its task. Elevation is a regression target and habitat a classification target.

dataset <- resolve.dataset.frame(
  header = plots,
  species = species,
  roles = list(plot_id = "plot_id", species_id = "species",
               abundance = "cover", genus = "genus", family = "family"),
  targets = list(
    elevation = list(column = "elevation", task = "regression"),
    habitat = list(column = "habitat", task = "classification")
  )
)
roles = rc.RoleMapping()
roles.plot_id = "plot_id"
roles.species_id = "species"
roles.abundance = "cover"
roles.genus = "genus"
roles.family = "family"

targets = [rc.TargetSpec.regression("elevation"),
           rc.TargetSpec.classification("habitat", 4)]
dataset = rc.ResolveDataset.from_pandas(plots, species, roles, targets)

The coordinates stay out of the roles here, so the predictions come from the species alone.

Training

Training holds out 20 % of the plots, drawn at random with a fixed seed, and stops when the loss on them no longer improves. The metrics are computed on these held-out plots.

resolve.manual_seed(42)
fit <- resolve.train.dataset(dataset, verbose = FALSE)
metrics <- fit$result$final_metrics
round(unlist(metrics$elevation[c("mae", "rmse", "r2", "band_25")]), 3)
#>     mae    rmse      r2 band_25 
#> 247.110 317.298   0.691   0.600
round(metrics$habitat$accuracy, 3)
#> [1] 0.8
rc.manual_seed(42)
model = rc.ResolveModel(dataset.schema, rc.model_config_for_dataset(dataset))
trainer = rc.Trainer(model, rc.TrainConfig())
trainer.prepare_data(dataset)
result = trainer.fit()
metrics = result.final_metrics
{name: round(metrics["elevation"][name], 3) for name in ["mae", "rmse", "r2", "band_25"]}
#> {'mae': 260.756, 'rmse': 301.784, 'r2': 0.721, 'band_25': 0.433}
round(metrics["habitat"]["accuracy"], 3)
#> 0.8

For elevation, mae and rmse are in metres, r2 is the share of the variance the predictions explain, and band_25 is the share of plots predicted within 25 % of their elevation; band_10 and band_50 give the same at 10 and 50 %. For habitat, accuracy is the share of plots assigned their recorded habitat, and the per-class precision, recall and F1 scores sit beside it in the same list. Training’s own seed fixes the held-out plots and the order the training plots are drawn in, and resolve.manual_seed() (rc.manual_seed() in Python) fixes the starting weights, so the same run on the same machine ends at the same numbers. The R and the Python run here still end at slightly different numbers, since each reaches the engine through its own torch build.

Predicting new plots

A saved model carries the species vocabulary it was trained with, so a new table is encoded against the same species. Here the model predicts the survey’s own plots again.

path <- file.path(tempdir(), "model.pt")
resolve.save(fit$trainer, path)

predictor <- resolve.load(path)
preds <- resolve.predict.dataset(predictor, dataset)
head(data.frame(plot = preds$plot_ids,
                elevation = round(preds$predictions$elevation),
                observed = plots$elevation[match(preds$plot_ids, plots$plot_id)]))
#>   plot elevation observed
#> 1 A001      2258     2188
#> 2 A002      1283      568
#> 3 A003      1969     2129
#> 4 A004      2284     2267
#> 5 A005      2074     2145
#> 6 A006      1785     1799
import os, tempfile

path = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "model.pt")
trainer.save(path)

predictor = rc.Predictor.load(path)
preds = predictor.predict_dataset(dataset)
out = pd.DataFrame({"plot": preds.plot_ids,
                    "elevation": preds.predictions["elevation"].numpy().round().astype(int)})
out.merge(plots[["plot_id", "elevation"]], left_on="plot", right_on="plot_id",
          suffixes=("", "_observed")).drop(columns="plot_id").head(6)
#>    plot  elevation  elevation_observed
#> 0  A001       2248                2188
#> 1  A002       1002                 568
#> 2  A003       2105                2129
#> 3  A004       2319                2267
#> 4  A005       2004                2145
#> 5  A006       1950                1799

A plot with a species the model never saw still gets a prediction: the unknown species is encoded through its genus and family where those are known.
